_about: Ruling 236.2 (the design director, b545, b549, b550): air campaigns, the grand campaign with the switch g.flags.ac on. A campaign is a standing order to an air force, flown every month until it is called off. 'sky': the battle for the sky over a province is held once the side fighting for it has had 'own' (airwar.json sky.own, b446's 1.5 to 1) times the defender's aircraft in reach over it for 'months' months running, or has won the fight itself each of those months where the defender has radar over its own ground (b446's guard), or at once when the defender's airfields there are knocked out (every fighter group in reach grounded, its field wrecked, or worn to readiness 'knocked', the floor, on a field this side has bombed since last month); held, it stays held while the holder keeps 'keep' times the defender's numbers and fights there at least every 'idle' + 1 months. 'stock': the damage bombs leave in a province carries over (every raid, b549) and comes back each month at the historian's rate for the target ('repair', air-campaign-236: 'perMonth', and 'dispersed' for Germany from 'dispersal.from'), at most 'most' of its output held down. 'use' says which repair row each raid reads: a raid by night is an area raid on the city's works, a raid by day a precision raid on its works ('aircraft'), an oilfield's refinery, or the fuel plants of a works province when the campaign aims at oil. 'dispersal': from March 1944 Germany's works were spread out: each raid on them does 'cut' of what it did (the feature builder's reading: the historian gives no number), and they come back at the 'dispersed' rate. 'will': each city or capital whose works are held down wears its country's will to fight by 'per' times the share held down, 'most' at most for the country (b549: small; bombing never broke a nation by itself). 'book': the historian's 54 doctrine rows, as he wrote them, read two ways (b549): at the stops that follow the book, each row's 'fly' phases open and close on their months for every country the player does not fly, on the provinces named (a province not on the map is passed over); at stops 3 to 5 the computer-opponent builder's staff reads them as doctrine. A row without 'fly' says in 'book' why the book does not open it as a campaign. 'share' is the part of the country's groups of that kind in reach of the targets that the campaign takes (1 all); 'bombers' puts its bombers in reach on a fight for the sky (raids on the airfields); 'escort' is the part of its fighters in reach that ride with a day raid; 'aim' oil or rail; 'kind' sky over the row's own kind. 'bands': the loss bands the record's commanders bore, a raid's losses over what it sent (the historian's part 4).
onAbout: A new grand campaign opens with air campaigns flown (g.flags.ac), as the design director ruled on 22 November (b623, b636). Read by name at the start (airCampaignsShipped). Scenarios, history campaigns and saved games keep what they had.

bands.words: Heavier than any air force bore: every one stopped within one to three raids.
Heavy: air forces flying at this rate stopped or changed course within a month or two.
Bearable while new aircraft and crews matched the losses: about 5% a raid could be kept up, 7% for long could not.
Light: kept up as long as there were targets.

airfield.firstRaid: runways and grass in hours to 2 days; aircraft and buildings in weeks
airfield.repeat: Had to be hit again daily or near it to keep shut; Manston was given up after August 1940's raids

track.repeat: Cut lines stayed cut only under daily attack

yard.firstRaid: through traffic in 2 to 7 days; full in 2 to 4 weeks
yard.repeat: Under the Transportation Plan (April to June 1944) French rail traffic fell to about a third; German car loadings fell by about half from August to December 1944, and further by March 1945

bridge.firstRaid: 3 to 8 weeks (ferries and pontoons in days)
bridge.repeat: The Seine bridges below Paris were all down by D-Day

port.firstRaid: most of its capacity in 1 to 3 weeks; months if sunken ships or mines block the channel
port.repeat: Liverpool lost about half its capacity for some days after May 1941; Japan's ports were shut by mines in 1945, which repair could not lift

aircraft.firstRaid: most output back in 4 to 8 weeks; machine tools mostly survived the buildings
aircraft.repeat: After Big Week (February 1944) German fighter output fell for about two months and then rose to its peak in September 1944

engines.repeat: Japan's Nakajima engine works at Musashino kept building through eight raids from November 1944

bearings.firstRaid: 3 to 6 months to full at the works
bearings.repeat: Stocks, imports from Sweden and Switzerland, redesign and dispersal meant no weapon went short (the bombing survey)

tanks.repeat: German tank output peaked in December 1944; Gorky's motor works, bombed in June 1943, was back in about three months

synthetic.firstRaid: partial in 2 to 3 weeks, full in 4 to 8
synthetic.repeat: Under raids every 2 to 4 weeks from 12 May 1944 it never came back: German aviation fuel fell from about 175,000 tons in April 1944 to about 10,000 tons by September, with some recovery in November before falling again; 350,000 men were put to repairs

refinery.repeat: Ploesti had spare capacity and was back above its old output within weeks of 1 Aug 1943; the 1944 campaign, raid after raid, cut it to about a fifth by August

steel.repeat: The Battle of the Ruhr (1943) cost Germany some months' growth in steel, not its supply

power.repeat: Seldom attacked; the bombing survey judged the German grid a missed target

city.firstRaid: main works back to about 80% in 2 to 5 months
city.repeat: Hamburg (July 1943) was back to about 80% in five months; Coventry's works mostly back in 6 to 8 weeks after November 1940. Japan's cities burned in 1945 did not come back, short of everything

bookAbout: Rider b569 (3) and (4), with the historian's shares and bases (historian/air-shares-b569.json and .md): at the stops that follow the book a row takes its 'share' (dated rows [from turn, share]) of the front-line aircraft of its nation's 'theatre', of every kind together, as the historian gives it; a bombing row fills it with bombers, a fight for the sky with each kind it flies at that share. Its escort takes 'escort' of the theatre's fighters (the feature builder's reading). A theatre is: Germany's west, east and Mediterranean by 'split' (the historian's whole-Luftwaffe split by date); the RAF at home, its groups on British home ground; America's Europe and Pacific, its groups on either side of the world; any other nation's, its whole air force. Groups are whole: a row takes one, and another only while that comes nearer its share than stopping does. Groups in reach of the row's targets go first. A group out of reach is moved on the row's month to the field its side holds nearest any of the row's 'bases' for that month, in reach of the targets, one with room first; if the side holds none, the row flies without it.
sources: Tooze, The Wages of Destruction (2006); Wagenfuehr's armaments series in the US Strategic Bombing Survey, The Effects of Strategic Bombing on the German War Economy (1945)
Harrison (ed.), The Economics of World War II (1998); Harrison, Accounting for War (1996)
War Production Board, Wartime Production Achievements and the Reconversion Outlook (1945)
US Strategic Bombing Survey, The Effects of Strategic Bombing on Japan's War Economy (1946); Cohen, Japan's Economy in War and Reconstruction (1949)
Middlebrook and Everitt, The Bomber Command War Diaries (1985); Webster and Frankland, The Strategic Air Offensive against Germany (HMSO, 1961)
Craven and Cate, The Army Air Forces in World War II; Freeman, The Mighty Eighth War Diary (1981)
Overy, The Air War 1939-1945 (1980) and The Bombing War (2013); Hardesty, Red Phoenix (1982); Bergerud, Fire in the Sky (2000)

fields._about: Rider b574 (the design director, 22:11Z) and the historian's list (historian/med-airfields-b574.md): the record's Mediterranean air war was flown from fields today's chart does not seed. With the switch on, these provinces have an airfield of at least this class (1 a landing ground, 2 an airfield, 3 an air base; airwar.json fields.sizes) all war; every one existed all war and served whoever held the province, so whoever holds it in the game uses it, as everywhere. With the switch off they are not read. Pantelleria is not on the chart: it folds into Sicily, which has its air base. Gambut is counted with Tobruk's El Adem.

radar._about: Ruling 236 riders b553 and b558 (Brian, 20:43Z: "if you had radar then your fighters are much better at intercepting bombing raids"), inside the switch; the historian's rows, historian/radar-night-b553.json. (a) Warning: the record's two chains (air.json radar.chains: Chain Home from 1, the Kammhuber Line from 24) stay on their months at every stop. At the stops that follow the book each other great power's chain comes in on its 'record' row's month whatever its research, over the row's 'regions' only where it names them ('where' is the card's phrase for that ground; 'plural' makes the raid report say 'give warning'). At stops 3 to 5 a nation holding Early-warning radar ('tech') has a chain over all the ground it holds, catching 'ground' of what a raid on its fields would. Without a chain only air.json radar.without (7 in 10) of the defending fighters meet a raid. (b) 'night': what a nation's fighters count for by night, as a share of their worth by day, in place of air.json combat.night.fighters (0.03): the historian's dated rows [from turn, figure], a row holding until the next. At the stops that follow the book they run by date; at stops 3 to 5 Fighter control ('control') is the gate: without it the nation keeps its first figure, with it the figure for the month. The regions are the historian's (historian/radar-night-b553.json, regions_b558); the optional middle Soviet step of August 1942 (six cities) is left out, as the director ruled. (c) b569(2): at stops 3 to 5 a staff whose ground was bombed by night within 'need' months takes Fighter control first in its research, once it holds Early-warning radar, every nation alike.

nightWhy.UK: 1 to 16: no ground control at night and no working airborne radar (the AI Mk III Blenheims). 17: the first ground-control (GCI) stations and the Beaufighter with AI Mk IV. 19: the two together, March 1941, rising to the best month of the Blitz in May 1941. 41: centimetric radar in Mosquitos (from early 1943). 53: Mosquitos with AI Mk VIII and X against Steinbock, 1944.
nightWhy.GER: 1 to 13: searchlights and few night fighters. 14: the searchlight belt and Freya line (October 1940), then the Himmelbett boxes in 1941. 30: Lichtenstein airborne radar in service (February 1942), general by late 1942. 41: the full Himmelbett and Lichtenstein system of 1943. 47: Window blinds Wuerzburg and Lichtenstein (Hamburg, 24/25 Jul 1943) for about two months. 49: free hunting in the bomber stream (Tame Boar and Wild Boar) with SN-2 radar, the peak of the night defence. 57: France's warning lost after D-Day, fuel short, British intruders and jamming. 63: the collapse of late 1944 and 1945.
nightWhy.USA: No night raids on American soil. Overseas, the P-70 and early navy night fighters to 1944; the P-61 with SCR-720 radar from mid-1944 (58).
nightWhy.SOV: Night fighters without radar, under searchlights, most of the war; most German night losses over Soviet cities were to guns.
nightWhy.JAP: Night fighters with upward-firing guns and few radar sets against the B-29 fire raids from 1944.
nightWhy.ITA: No night-fighter arm of note; German night fighters in Italy in 1943.

gunners._about: Rulings 237 b557 and b559 (accepted), the historian's historian/gunner-kills-b557.md: the defending fighters the bombers' gunners bring down, for each bomber the fighters bring down (real losses, never the gunners' claims). With the switch on these take the place of ruling 227's day figure (airwar.json day.kill x the nation's bomber defence); with it off 227 stands as it is. The game flies one kind of bomber a nation, so the historian's kinds are read from what the game knows ('map'). 'night': any bomber by night. 'ground': a strike on troops ('ground' and 'line'), the two-seat ground-attack aircraft with a rear gunner. 'box': the nations whose day bombers fly as heavy boxes, 'alone' when no escort reached the target, 'escorted' when one did (keyed by the raid's escort, not the year, so it works at every stop). 'b29': that nation's day raids from 'from' on Japan's home islands ('regions', held by 'vs'); elsewhere its heavy-box rows stand (the historian, 21:08Z: the B-24s and B-25s flew the day raids on the Philippines, New Guinea, Borneo and Formosa). 'day': every other day raid, by nation, rows [from turn, ratio] (a row holds until the next).

map.Light and medium bombers with hand-held: Every nation's day bombers from September 1939 to December 1941 (turns 1 to 28), and Britain's in 1941 (17 to 28: the Blenheims' day raids).
map.Bombers with power turrets by day, 1939-: Britain's day bombers from September 1939 to December 1940 (1 to 16: the Wellingtons and Hampdens).
map.Medium bombers in formation with more gu: Every nation's day bombers from January 1942 (29), America's excepted.
map.Heavy bomber boxes (0.4 beyond escort, 0: America's day bombers, every month, keyed by whether an escort reached the target. The game's one American bomber is the heavy; its B-25s and B-26s are not told apart.
map.B-29 by day over Japan (0.5): America's day raids on Japan's home islands while Japan holds them, from June 1944 (58); elsewhere the heavy-box rows.
map.Ground-attack aircraft with a rear gunne: Every nation's strikes on troops ('ground' and 'line'), whatever the year: the game's bombers flying close support stand for the Il-2s and Ju 87s.
